strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: accelerating continuous-token autoregressive image generation without additional training. Adapting speculative decoding to diffusion-based token generators is a worthwhile direction.

The reported practical results are promising. Table 1 covers three draft–target pairings and four batch sizes, with speedups reaching 2.33× and 1.44× at batch size one. Table 2 reports close FID/IS results, supported by 50,000-image evaluations and repeated runs.

The paper provides useful ablations of trajectory alignment, draft length, pre-filling, guidance, and temperature. The integral-free residual rejection sampler in Eq. (10) is valid when supplied with the actual normalized target and proposal densities.
weaknesses: The central density-ratio derivation is mathematically unsound. Eq. (1), repeated in supplementary Eq. (12), identifies an endpoint conditional density with a product of transition densities. That product describes a complete diffusion trajectory; obtaining the endpoint density requires integrating over intermediate states. Consequently, Eq. (5) is not established as the token-density ratio required by speculative decoding. Supplement A.3 proves the standard acceptance/residual-sampling identity assuming correct densities, but does not justify the densities actually used. This undermines the paper’s central distribution-preservation claim.

Trajectory alignment introduces a second unresolved issue. The Gaussian exponential cancellation compares densities evaluated at different model-specific states, x_t^p and x_t^q. Sharing Gaussian noise does not turn this into a likelihood ratio at the same sample. A valid auxiliary-variable construction would need explicitly defined distributions, transformations, and a matching residual sampler. Algorithm 1 instead resamples only from the final-step conditional while retaining the trajectory-dependent covariance multiplier; its equivalence to sampling the claimed residual distribution is unproved.

The experiments support approximate image-quality preservation, not equality of output distributions. Similar FID/IS values cannot validate the theoretical claim in Section 4.2. Moreover, Section 4.3 attributes artifacts to omitting pre-filling and improved quality to alignment, although an exact sampler should preserve the target distribution under either configuration. Controlled tests on analytically tractable diffusion chains would be particularly valuable for checking the proposed acceptance rule.

The speed–quality evidence is incomplete. Table 2 does not identify its draft length or pre-filling configuration, so its quality measurements cannot be confidently associated with the headline 2.33× setting. There is no quantitative quality-versus-speed sweep or comparison with reducing MAR generation steps. Evaluation on one model family and one resolution also limits the broader claims about continuous-valued autoregressive generators.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. MAR uses bidirectional attention, so parallel verification must explain how each token receives exactly its intended prefix without future-token leakage, and account for the resulting computation. Supplement C does not adequately specify this mechanism. Algorithm 1 also references p_n when rejection follows n accepted tokens, rather than p_{n+1}, and leaves the returned extra token undefined when all drafts are accepted. These pseudocode issues are repairable, but further impede reproducibility alongside the missing code link.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: accelerating continuous-token autoregressive image generation without additional training. Extending speculative decoding to diffusion-based token generators is a relevant computer-vision research direction.

The reported results are practically promising. Table 1 covers multiple model pairs, draft lengths, and batch sizes, with speedups reaching 2.33× at batch size 256 and 1.44× at batch size 1. Table 2 reports FID and IS close to the target models, using 50,000 generated images and repeated evaluations.

The residual rejection-sampling construction in Eqs. (6)–(10) is valid when exact, normalized target and proposal densities are available: proposing from p and accepting with max(0, 1−q/p) avoids computing the residual normalizer. The alignment, pre-filling, guidance, and temperature experiments also provide useful empirical observations.
weaknesses: The central density-ratio derivation is incorrect as written. Eqs. (1) and (12) identify an endpoint conditional density with a product of transition densities along one sampled diffusion trajectory. That product describes a trajectory density; obtaining the endpoint density requires integrating out intermediate states. Consequently, the proposed calculation does not establish the token-level p(x)/q(x) needed for exact speculative decoding. Appendix A.3 proves the standard acceptance/residual identity assuming correct densities, but does not repair this foundational gap.

Trajectory alignment introduces a second unresolved issue. The cancellation preceding Eq. (4) evaluates target and draft transition densities at different states, x^p and x^q. Sharing Gaussian noise can cancel exponential terms at these separately transformed points, but this does not establish a likelihood ratio at a common sample. An auxiliary-variable formulation could potentially justify an alternative method, but the paper supplies neither the requisite common-space density argument nor a justification for its accumulated variance factor. These are substantive problems with the claimed distribution-preservation guarantee, rather than notation corrections.

The experiments support comparable image quality, not equality of output distributions. Similar FID/IS values cannot validate the disputed density calculation, despite the stronger interpretation in Section 4.2. Table 2 also does not identify the draft length and pre-filling configuration, leaving its connection to the maximum-speedup setting unclear. A tractable diffusion example with known endpoint densities and direct distributional checks would be particularly valuable. The reported removal of artifacts through alignment and pre-filling also deserves reconciliation with the claim that all these variants preserve the same target distribution.

Essential implementation details for both correctness and runtime are missing. Appendix C does not explain how bidirectional MAR verification computes each draft token's correct prefix-conditioned distribution in parallel without access to later draft tokens, or how different rejection positions are handled across a batch. Algorithm 1 leaves the returned extra token undefined when all drafts are accepted and uses p_n for the correction after n accepted tokens, although the rejected position is n+1. These pseudocode errors are individually repairable, but the incomplete verification procedure and absent code link materially limit reproducibility.

The evidence does not yet establish a compelling alternative approximate-acceleration contribution if exactness is withdrawn. Evaluation is restricted to MAR on ImageNet 256×256, with no quality–latency comparison against simply reducing MAR generation steps. Absolute latency, memory costs, and verification overhead are not reported. Moreover, Table 4 shows that pre-filling generally leaves speed unchanged or slightly worsens it, so its increased acceptance rate does not demonstrate an acceleration benefit. The useful empirical results therefore do not compensate for the failure to substantiate the paper's central lossless-decoding claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: accelerating continuous-token autoregressive image generation without additional training. Adapting speculative decoding to diffusion-based token generators is a worthwhile research direction.

The reported practical results are promising. Table 1 covers three draft–target pairings and four batch sizes, with speedups reaching 2.33×. Table 2 reports FID and IS close to the target models, supported by 50,000-image evaluations and repeated runs.

The residual-distribution rejection sampler in Equations (6)–(10) is valid when exact target and proposal densities are available. Ablations on trajectory alignment, pre-filling, guidance, and temperature provide useful empirical observations.
weaknesses: The central density-ratio derivation is incorrect as written. Equation (1), repeated in Equation (12), equates an endpoint conditional density with a product describing an entire diffusion trajectory. Obtaining the endpoint density requires integrating over intermediate states. Furthermore, Equations (3)–(5) cancel Gaussian terms evaluated at different draft and target trajectory points; this does not establish the likelihood ratio at the same proposed sample required by speculative decoding. Shared noise alone does not justify this substitution. Appendix A.3 proves correctness assuming valid densities, so it does not resolve this foundational gap in the claimed distribution-preservation guarantee.

The implemented residual sampler is not shown to match the theoretical sampler. Algorithm 1 repeatedly samples only the final Gaussian conditional while retaining intermediate trajectories and the determinant factor, whereas Section 3.3 requires proposals from the target distribution used in the density ratio. A rigorous auxiliary-variable formulation could potentially justify a related approach, but none is supplied. The pseudocode also uses index n after accepting n tokens, rather than the rejected position n+1, and leaves the returned extra token undefined when all drafts are accepted.

The empirical evidence supports comparable image quality, not exact distribution preservation. Similar FID/IS values cannot validate the disputed likelihood ratio. Table 2 also omits the draft length, preventing a clear association between its quality measurements and the maximum reported speedup. Controlled experiments with analytically tractable diffusion chains would help test correctness directly.

The practical acceleration case remains incompletely characterized. Results cover only MAR on ImageNet at 256×256, report relative speedups without absolute latency or memory costs, and do not explain sufficiently how parallel verification preserves each prefix's conditioning under MAR's bidirectional attention. Table 4 generally shows unchanged or slightly worse speed with pre-filling despite increased acceptance, weakening its claimed efficiency benefit. These issues are secondary to the invalid density derivation, which prevents acceptance under the Algorithms/General criteria.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: accelerating continuous autoregressive image generation without additional training. Integrating speculative decoding with diffusion-based token generators is a potentially useful contribution.

The reported timing evaluation spans MAR, xAR, and Harmon, multiple batch sizes, and two resolutions for Harmon. Tables 1–2 report substantial gains, including 2.33× for MAR and 2.54× for Harmon, while also documenting more modest single-image gains.

Table 3 provides encouraging evidence of comparable MAR image quality, with FID and IS evaluated on 50,000 images and variability reported. The trajectory-alignment ablation, sampling-overhead measurements, and discussion of draft-model costs provide useful empirical context.
weaknesses: The central distribution-preservation claim rests on an incorrect density identity. Equations 1–2 equate the output-token density with p(x_T) times the product of reverse-transition densities. This product is the joint density of the entire diffusion trajectory; obtaining p(x_0) requires integrating out intermediate states and initial noise. Even conditional on x_T, intermediate states must be marginalized. Appendix A repeats this error, while Appendix A.3 proves only the standard speculative-sampling identity assuming access to correct p and q. It therefore does not establish correctness of the implemented method.

Trajectory alignment does not justify the proposed likelihood-ratio simplification. Equation 6 evaluates target and draft transition densities at different, coupled samples. Cancellation of their noise terms does not produce the density ratio at the same proposed sample required by speculative decoding. Theorem 1 concerns expected distance under a coupling; reducing this distance does not itself change the marginal distributions or establish increased marginal overlap. A valid augmented-variable or conditional-sampling formulation would require a separate derivation, including the appropriate density transformations.

The efficient rejection sampler is consequently unproven. Equations 9–11 are valid when proposals are drawn from the actual target distribution and correct densities are available. Equation 12 instead repeatedly samples the final Gaussian conditional while holding preceding trajectories fixed and retaining the trajectory-dependent determinant factor. The manuscript does not establish that this procedure samples the required residual distribution. This is consequential because avoiding repeated diffusion inference is central to the reported efficiency.

The empirical evidence cannot substitute for the missing correctness guarantee. Similar FID and IS do not demonstrate equality of output distributions, and quantitative quality evaluation is reported only for MAR, despite speed and quality-preservation claims covering xAR and Harmon. Controlled examples with analytically known output densities would directly test the acceptance and resampling rules; quality measurements across draft lengths and all three model families are also needed.

The practical baseline comparison is incomplete. Appendix D changes xAR from its native four-step generation to token-by-token generation, so the reported speedups do not establish acceleration over its native inference configuration. For MAR, Table 8 already reports 1.99× acceleration with FID 1.56 using two-token masked generation, which is competitive with the proposed method's reported quality. Matched quality–latency comparisons with native generation schedules are needed to establish the practical advantage.

The evidence for token pre-filling is weak: Table 5 shows no speed improvement over 0% pre-filling, and some settings become slower. Its acceptance-rate benefit is also inconsistent, including a decrease from 0.33 to 0.31 at draft length 8 with 5% pre-filling. These results do not support presenting it as an established acceleration contribution.

Reproducibility needs clarification. The abstract's code-availability statement has no link, and Algorithm 1 uses p_n and q_n after accepting n tokens, although the rejected position should be n+1; it also returns an undefined extra token when all drafts are accepted. These are repairable presentation issues, but the density and sampling problems above require substantive changes. Under Algorithms/General, the promising timing results do not outweigh the unsupported core guarantee.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: accelerating continuous autoregressive image generation without additional training. Integration with pretrained MAR, xAR, and Harmon makes the proposed direction practically relevant.

Tables 1–2 report substantial wall-clock improvements across batch sizes, including peak speedups of 2.33×, 2.72×, and 2.54×. Table 3 provides encouraging evidence of comparable MAR generation quality, with FID/IS results and variability estimates.

The continuous residual-sampling identity in Equations 9–11 is valid when exact target and proposal densities are available. The alignment, pre-filling, guidance, and sampling-overhead ablations also provide useful empirical observations.
weaknesses: The central distribution-preservation claim is not established. Equations 1–2 identify a product of diffusion transition densities with the output-token density. That product describes a joint trajectory density; obtaining the endpoint density requires integrating out intermediate states. Appendix A.3 proves the standard speculative-sampling identity assuming correct densities, but does not justify the densities actually used by this algorithm. This is a consequential technical gap for an Algorithms/General submission claiming lossless acceleration.

Trajectory alignment does not repair this gap. Equation 6 compares densities at different, coupled states, whereas the speculative acceptance ratio requires densities of the same proposal under a properly defined probability space. Shared noise can reduce paired sample distances without changing either marginal distribution or their overlap. Consequently, Theorem 1 does not establish the claimed increase in exact marginal acceptance probability. A valid auxiliary-variable formulation would require its own acceptance rule and proof, including any necessary change-of-variable factors.

The efficient rejection sampler introduces another unsupported step. Following Equation 12, the method repeatedly samples only the final Gaussian conditional while holding intermediate trajectories fixed, instead of sampling the full target distribution used in Equation 11. The manuscript does not establish that this procedure produces the required residual distribution. Because this shortcut enables negligible resampling overhead, its correctness directly affects both the quality guarantee and the acceleration argument.

Experimental quality validation is insufficient to support the breadth of the claims. Quantitative FID/IS comparisons are reported only for MAR; xAR and Harmon receive speed measurements without corresponding quantitative quality or text-alignment evaluation. Table 3 also does not specify draft length, preventing a clear association between quality and the fastest configurations. Similar FID/IS values cannot validate exact distribution preservation.

The practical baseline comparison needs strengthening. Appendix D changes xAR from its original four-step next-cell generation to tokenwise generation, so the reported speedups do not establish improvements over its normal inference configuration. For MAR, Table 8 already shows a simple masked-generation setting achieving 1.99× speedup with FID 1.56, comparable to the reported speculative results. A matched quality–latency comparison is necessary to establish the method's practical advantage.

Reproducibility and component-level evidence remain incomplete. Algorithm 1 uses p_n for the rejected position although n denotes the number of accepted drafts, and leaves the returned extra token undefined when all drafts are accepted. The abstract's code-availability statement contains no link. Separately, Table 5 shows pre-filling matching or slightly reducing speed despite higher acceptance in some settings, so its claimed acceleration benefit is not demonstrated. These issues are secondary to the fundamental density and sampling errors.

strengths: The paper addresses an important efficiency bottleneck in continuous autoregressive image generation. Integrating speculative decoding into pretrained models without additional training is practically appealing.

Experiments report meaningful wall-clock improvements across MAR, xAR, and Harmon, with maximum speedups of 2.33×, 2.72×, and 2.54×, respectively. Reporting multiple batch sizes and resolutions provides useful evidence about operating conditions.

MAR quality results are encouraging: Table 3 reports FID and IS close to the target-model baselines, with repeated evaluations and variability estimates. Ablations examine trajectory alignment, pre-filling, draft length, temperature, and guidance, while the appendix acknowledges limitations from draft-model overhead.
weaknesses: The central distribution-preservation claim is not established. Equations 1–2 identify a product of diffusion transition densities with the output-token density; that product describes a joint trajectory density, whereas the output density requires marginalizing intermediate states. Equation 8 additionally evaluates target and draft transitions along different trajectories. Appendix A.3 proves the standard speculative-sampling identity assuming correct densities and residual sampling, but does not justify these substitutions. This is a substantive soundness concern for an Algorithms/General contribution claiming lossless acceleration.

Trajectory alignment and residual resampling need a consistent probabilistic formulation. Sharing noise can reduce the distance between paired samples without changing either marginal distribution, so Theorem 1 alone does not establish increased marginal distribution overlap. Moreover, Section 3.3 replaces sampling from the target output distribution with repeated sampling from a fixed final-step Gaussian while retaining the trajectory determinant factor. A derivation conditioning on shared auxiliary randomness, including the appropriate density or change-of-variables accounting, is needed to establish correctness. Similar FID and IS cannot verify exact distribution preservation.

Quality-preservation evidence is substantially narrower than the acceleration evidence. Quantitative quality results are provided for MAR, but not for xAR or Harmon, including Harmon's 512-resolution setting. Table 3 also does not specify the draft length. Quality measurements paired with the speed configurations are needed to support the broad claim of acceleration without degradation.

The practical baseline comparison needs clearer qualification. Appendix D changes xAR from its native four-step generation to next-token generation, so the reported speedup does not establish an advantage over its default inference configuration. Appendix G.5 supplies a useful MAR masked-generation comparison, but a matched latency–quality comparison against native model configurations would better establish practical impact. Furthermore, Table 5 shows that pre-filling leaves speed unchanged or slightly worsens it, despite its claimed role in acceleration.

Reproducibility and algorithm presentation need improvement. The abstract's code-availability statement has no link. Algorithm 1 appears to use the accepted-token count n rather than the rejected position n+1 for resampling, permits an undefined zero index, and leaves the extra token undefined when all drafts are accepted. These are potentially correctable presentation issues, but the implementation details must also explain how parallel verification preserves each token's intended prefix under MAR's bidirectional attention.
